title: Live-SWE-agent: Can Software Engineering Agents Self-Evolve on the Fly?
mutable_substrate: Task-local executable Python helper scripts created, revised, and invoked inside one issue-solving trajectory. The evaluated implementation leaves the mini-SWE-agent loop, system workflow, model weights, and persistent cross-task scaffold unchanged; broader prompt and workflow rewriting is future work.
optimization_operator: The same task-solving LLM writes or edits a Python script through its ordinary one-command shell interface after an initial tool-creation instruction and repeated reflection reminders. Tool synthesis is interleaved with repository inspection, editing, testing, and patch submission; there is no separate meta-agent, population search, or weight update.
feedback_selection: Command return codes, truncated command output, repository tests, and the issue trajectory guide tool creation and revision. A feedback prompt after every step asks whether a tool would help. Tools are not independently scored or selected; final benchmark patch resolution is a post-hoc aggregate outcome rather than an online fitness function.
archive_memory: Within-task memory consists of generated script files and the conversational trajectory. The reported system has no archive, lineage, retrieval index, or cross-task persistence; saving tools and insights as reusable skills is proposed as future work.
validation_strategy: Single-attempt, one-patch-per-issue evaluation on all 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks and 731 public SWE-Bench Pro tasks, plus a 50-task SWE-bench Multilingual subset. Paired mini-SWE-agent comparisons vary four full-Verified backends; a shared random 50-task Verified subset ablates tool creation, reflection, and six model backends. A prior 60-task subset compares reported performance and offline cost with SICA, DGM, and HGM.
adaptation_mode: Online, runtime, within-task adaptation with ephemeral tools. It incurs per-issue inference and execution cost but no benchmark-wide offline evolution. It is not continual across tasks in the evaluated implementation.
benchmarks: SWE-Bench Pro public set: 731 issues across 11 repositories and Python, Go, TypeScript, and JavaScript
SWE-bench Verified-60 subset used by prior self-improving-agent comparisons
Random 50-task SWE-bench Verified component and backend ablation subset
50-task SWE-bench Multilingual subset spanning nine programming languages
principal_results: On full SWE-bench Verified, Live-SWE-agent improves over mini-SWE-agent from 59.8% to 63.0% with GPT-5-Mini, 65.0% to 68.4% with GPT-5, 70.6% to 75.4% with Claude 4.5 Sonnet, and 74.2% to 77.4% with Gemini 3 Pro.
On SWE-Bench Pro with Claude 4.5 Sonnet, Live-SWE-agent resolves 45.8% versus SWE-agent's 43.6%, with average Live cost of $0.73 per issue.
On Verified-60 with GPT-5-Mini, Live-SWE-agent reaches 65.0% with zero offline hours, versus SICA 50.0%, DGM 53.3% at 1,231 offline hours, and HGM 56.7% at 512 offline hours.
On the 50-task component subset, no tool creation scores 62.0%, tool permission without reflection 64.0%, and full Live-SWE-agent 76.0%; mean tool counts are 0.00, 2.92, and 3.28.

Backend ablation is mixed: GPT-5-Nano falls 44.0% to 14.0%, GPT-5-Mini falls 60.0% to 58.0%, GPT-5 rises 60.0% to 68.0%, Claude 3.7 rises 46.0% to 50.0%, Claude 4 rises 58.0% to 64.0%, and Claude 4.5 rises 62.0% to 76.0%.
On the 50-task Multilingual subset with Claude 4.5 Sonnet, resolution rises from 40.0% to 46.0%, while average issue cost rises from $0.59 to $0.66.
Generated tools include general editors and context-aware search, repository-specific MARC analyzers, and a Go analyzer used to solve a Pro issue missed by the compared baseline.
limitations: The current mutable substrate is limited to task-local tool scripts; the system does not rewrite its persistent prompt, loop, workflow, model, or cross-task memory despite broader self-evolution framing.
Generated tools are discarded after each task, so the reported method does not demonstrate cumulative or continual improvement across issues.
Tool synthesis hurts weaker backends: GPT-5-Nano loops and drops from 44.0% to 14.0%, while GPT-5-Mini also regresses on the 50-task ablation.
Single-patch results and one 50-task subset provide no run-to-run variance, confidence intervals, or repeated stochastic trials.
External self-improving-agent and leaderboard comparisons reuse reported results and are not controlled for total compute, runtime adaptation cost, or implementation differences.
The paper reports average dollar cost but not wall-clock latency, step counts, per-tool creation cost, tool execution frequency, or individual-tool causal attribution.
t-SNE tool plots and filename-derived categories are descriptive and have no clustering stability or success-correlation analysis.
Experiments remain within repository issue resolution; proposed test generation, security, binary analysis, and greenfield applications are not evaluated.
safety_controls: The mini-SWE-agent configuration limits each issue to 250 steps and a $3 cost cap.
The task prompt tells the model to modify non-test source files and not tests or configuration, although the paper does not describe independent enforcement.
Large command outputs are truncated to the first and last 5,000 characters to control context growth.
No dedicated security analysis, permission model, static checker, tool sandbox policy, secret-access evaluation, or immutable semantic verifier is reported for arbitrary generated Python scripts.

explicit_predecessors.name: mini-SWE-agent
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Direct implementation base and fixed-action comparison.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: Live-SWE-agent retains mini-SWE-agent's approximately 100-line loop, one-command interface, 250-step and $3 limits, and most of its prompt, adding tool instructions and per-step reflection.

explicit_predecessors.name: Self-Improving Coding Agent (SICA)
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit offline self-improvement predecessor and Verified-60 baseline.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The paper contrasts SICA's benchmark-wide offline scaffold evolution with task-local runtime tool creation and reports 50.0% versus Live-SWE-agent's 65.0% on the shared subset.

explicit_predecessors.name: Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM)
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit offline open-ended self-improvement predecessor and Verified-60 baseline.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The introduction motivates runtime adaptation partly through DGM's high offline cost; the comparison reports DGM at 53.3% and 1,231 offline hours versus Live-SWE-agent at 65.0% and zero offline hours.

explicit_predecessors.name: Huxley-Gödel Machine (HGM)
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit evaluator-directed self-improvement predecessor and strongest Verified-60 offline baseline.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The reported subset comparison gives HGM 56.7% and 512 offline hours, 8.3 percentage points below Live-SWE-agent.

explicit_predecessors.name: SWE-agent and OpenHands
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit fixed, handcrafted software-agent scaffold lineage and contrast.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: Related work frames these systems as LLMs equipped with predetermined coding tools; SWE-agent is the direct Pro baseline.

explicit_predecessors.name: LLM tool-creation systems
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The related-work section cites tool creation for general reasoning, embodied agents, and verifiable tasks, while positioning Live-SWE-agent as applying runtime synthesis to real repository repair.

open_questions: How should a runtime policy predict when tool synthesis will help rather than consume budget or induce loops?
Can tools be persisted across tasks with validation, provenance, retrieval, deprecation, and protection against cross-task contamination?
Do the gains survive repeated stochastic trials, different random task subsets, equalized total compute, and latency-aware evaluation?
Which individual tool properties—interface simplicity, feedback quality, specialization, or reuse—causally improve patch resolution?
How can arbitrary generated scripts be sandboxed and verified before they access repositories, credentials, networks, or persistent state?
Can the system safely modify its own prompt, context policy, and orchestration loop at runtime without corrupting the evaluator or submission protocol?
How should model evaluation distinguish base coding ability from the ability to construct a task-specific scaffold?
Will runtime self-evolution generalize beyond repository repair to testing, vulnerability analysis, binary tooling, and greenfield software creation?
